summary: This informational memo analyses the security threats relevant to the NSIS signalling protocols. It aims to help readers understand the security considerations in the NSIS requirements, framework and protocol documents.

eli5.summary: Before building a lock, you list how burglars might get in. This document lists the ways attackers could abuse NSIS signalling.

questions: what are the attacks on nsis signaling
what are the security threats to nsis
what is a man in the middle attack on signaling
what is session ownership in nsis
subtitle: A catalogue of the ways attackers could abuse the Next Steps in Signaling (NSIS) protocols, written before the protocols were finished.

tldr.problem: NSIS signaling installs state such as QoS reservations and firewall pinholes on nodes along a data path, so a weakly protected design would let attackers steal service, disrupt networks or hijack reservations.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lays out the communication models NSIS can use, then walks through four generic threats and eleven NSIS-specific threat scenarios, with examples of what each could do.
tldr.outcome: It describes no specific vulnerabilities and no fixes. It is a guide for designers, and it points to RFC 3726 for the security requirements meant to counter these threats.

today: RFC 4081 is an Informational memo published in June 2005, and the registry metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains a threat analysis for NSIS design, not a specification, and points to RFC 3726 for the related security requirements.

sections.title: Why a Threat Analysis
sections.content:
Whenever a protocol is developed or modified, its threats should be evaluated. This memo is one step in the NSIS working group's security work. It sits beside the analysis activities, the requirements in RFC 3726, the framework in RFC 4080 and the protocol suite itself (GIMPS, the NAT/Firewall NSLP and the QoS NSLP).

It identifies the basic threats that the design of the NSIS protocol suite has to address. It cannot cover every signaling application: the QoS and NAT/Firewall documents must each describe their own trust models and threats. Investigations of a specific architecture or context are out of scope, and the abstract says plainly that the memo does not describe vulnerabilities of specific parts of the suite.
sections.eli5: Before a team builds something new, they sit down and think about what could go wrong. This paper is that thinking-down-in-advance for NSIS.

sections.title: Who Talks to Whom
sections.content:
NSIS signals information from an NSIS Initiator to nodes along the path towards an NSIS Responder, so many entities are involved. The memo names the relationships because each has different trust and security needs. Trust here means a mutual a priori relationship in which the parties believe the others will behave correctly even in the future, and some trust in intermediate nodes is unavoidable: a complete lack of trust between participating entities makes NSIS signaling fail.

First-peer communication links the Initiator to the first NSIS-aware node. In roaming environments there may be no pre-established security association between those peers, while enterprise networks usually have a strong one. Intra-domain communication stays inside one administrative domain, where the authorization of the Initiator need not be repeated at every node and key management may be simpler, though protection is still needed against non-NSIS nodes. Inter-domain communication crosses domains, which can burden authorization and key management between networks that do not know each other in advance.

The memo also describes end-to-middle, middle-to-middle and end-to-end relationships. Protecting a whole message end-to-end is typically not required, and may not even be feasible, because intermediate NSIS nodes need to add, inspect, modify or delete objects in the message.
sections.eli5: A message may pass through many helpers on its way. Whether you can trust each helper changes how carefully you must lock the message, and some helpers need to open it to do their job.

sections.title: Generic Signaling Threats
sections.content:
The memo splits protection into two steps. The first, entity authentication and key establishment, produces a security association. The second, message protection, uses that association. The first step tends to be more expensive, which is why the two are separated.

The generic threats are:

  • Man-in-the-middle attacks. During association setup the adversary fools the Initiator about who it is authenticating to. This needs missing, unilateral or weak authentication. An attack is also possible in the discovery phase, where the adversary injects a bogus discovery reply so that a node sets up a messaging association with the adversary or with a node that is not on the path. The problem is self-healing, because discovery is repeated periodically, though a ping-pong behavior might result.
  • Replay of signaling messages. An adversary collects messages and replays them later or elsewhere. A harder variant crashes a node so it loses state such as sequence numbers, then replays old messages.
  • Injecting or modifying messages. Reordering, delaying, dropping, injecting or truncating messages. An injected request for a large amount of resources could cause other requests to be rejected.
  • Insecure parameter negotiation. Without protecting the negotiation, a downgrading attack can force weaker mechanisms than the parties want.
sections.eli5: A sneaky person might pretend to be your friend, replay an old note, scribble on a note you are passing, or trick you into using a weaker lock.

sections.title: Flooding, Denial of Service and Topology
sections.content:
Flooding is the first NSIS-specific scenario. The memo looks at several layers. Processing the Router Alert Option makes a router intercept packets, so a flood of bogus messages costs resources before they are dropped. The transport and NTLP layers can be attacked with bogus requests or by completing handshakes. At the signaling layer, an adversary can force storage (for example for fragmentation handling) or computation, such as verifying a random bit sequence passed off as a digital signature. Messages that are idempotent are particularly vulnerable, and incoming messages that trigger lookups at policy, LDAP or AAA servers can exhaust those servers.

The denial of service section adds three cases: sending many messages that allocate state along a path, abusing the discovery phase so signaling goes to nodes off the data path, and injecting false error or response messages. Finally, NSIS messages can be used for network mapping, which may conflict with an organization's wish not to disclose its topology, and with requirements for automatic discovery and diagnostics.
sections.eli5: Someone could shout so many fake requests at a helper that it has no time left for real ones, or ask so many questions that they learn the map of a building they should not see.

sections.title: Spoofing, Authorization and Ownership
sections.content:
Identity spoofing occurs in three forms: during association setup with weak authentication, by modifying the flow identifier in a signaling message, and by spoofing data traffic. The memo's example is a QoS reservation installed for the user Alice. The adversary Eve spoofs Alice's IP address and sends data that gets the reservation's preferential treatment, or passes through a firewall pinhole opened for Alice. Soft state helps only partly: Alice's absence is not noticed until a refresh is due.

Other threats in this group:

  • Unprotected authorization information. An authorization token returned unprotected to the end host could let an eavesdropper steal resources or watch communication patterns.
  • Missing non-repudiation. A user or provider could later deny a reservation. The memo notes that non-repudiation is not provided in today's networks and would add overhead.
  • Malicious NSIS entity. If an edge router is taken over, the whole network's security is compromised. A chain of trust is only as strong as its weakest link.
  • Unprotected session ownership. If an adversary learns a Session Identifier, it can send a message carrying it, and a cross-over router cannot tell whether the sender owns the session. The adversary could modify or delete the reservation.

Finally, attacks on the NTLP include header manipulation, session hijacking and unexpected aborts against unprotected transport protocols, and attacks on congestion control.
sections.eli5: If a thief copies your ticket number, a doorman may let them use your seat. The doorman cannot tell who really owns the ticket, so the ticket needs a way to prove its owner.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Takeaways
sections.content:
The whole memo is about security. It identifies the parts of an NSIS network (Initiator, Responder and the administrative domains between them), considers five communication cases and the trust presumed in each, and concludes that protocol security measures are needed for authentication, key exchange, message integrity, replay protection, confidentiality, authorization and some precautions against denial of service.

Not every threat is equally serious in every context. Because a designer cannot foresee all uses, the memo says a full range of security capabilities is needed, along with ways for users to negotiate and select what they need case by case. The security requirements meant to counter these threats are listed in RFC 3726.
sections.eli5: Different places need different amounts of protection, so the builders should offer many kinds of locks and let people pick the ones they need.

items.title: First-peer / last-peer
items.text: An end host and its nearest NSIS-aware node.

items.title: End-to-middle
items.text: An end entity and an intermediate node that is not its adjacent peer.

items.title: End-to-end
items.text: Initiator to Responder, usually not cryptographically protected as a whole.
